title: Why was Bresson such a huge Chaplin fan?

commenti.body:
I'm not sure that many Chaplin films would quite qualify as "filmed theater," at least in the way that Bresson means it here.

I think what Bresson is referring to the style of keeping things at arms length that was very popular, especially among Hollywood films, around the time that Bresson first started.

It's things like, a 30-40 second static shot of a telephone call, it's a wide shot of a person entering a room, a lighting cue as if there are stage hands pulling the lights.

I don't think Chaplin fits into these for a number of reasons. There are plenty of wide shots in his films, in fact they heavily rely on wide shots, but within these wide shots, he uses techniques that cannot be replicated in any other medium. Consider:

[https://cdn8.openculture.com/2020/11/04205751/chaplin-gif-1.gif](https://cdn8.openculture.com/2020/11/04205751/chaplin-gif-1.gif)

This shot is fairly "cinematic." It's just a wide shot with a pan. Nearly every film uses one, as do many of the "filmed theater" movies that Bresson despised, but the effect within the image is impossible to produce in another medium. 

Similarly, I think the sheer silliness of many of Chaplin's works does not lend itself to theater, or at least lend it's self to *being taken seriously* in the theater, which is what Chaplin's goal was. Sadly he wasn't until many years later, though.

It also seems quite common for extremely self-serious director like Bresson to randomly love comedies or totally odd movies for their style. Haneke, Tarkovsky and Bergman were also fans of Chaplin, and I think it's his use of pure filmmaking that they loved, but I also think being distracted from their seemingly constant dour and serious thoughts as well. 

Remember: one of Stanley Kubrick's favourite films was *White Men Can't Jump.* If doesn't show the complexity of personal taste, I don't know what does.

As far as the love for Chaplin goes, I can't think of a single filmmaker who dislikes his work. I know Orson Welles disliked Modern Times, and ultimately ranked Keaton above him, but he was also an enormous fan of City Lights (at one point it was cited as his favorite movie). From Andrei Tarkovsky to Vittorio De Sica to Jean Renoir, Chaplin may be the single most acclaimed filmmaker of all time.

As to the "Kubrick likes White Men Can't Jump," and the whole idea of serious directors liking comedies, this was brought up to Christian Bale when it was reported that his favorite movie was Beverly Hills Ninja. Bale admitted to liking it, but he also said that it was his default answer because if he were to say anything else, whether a serious movie, a popular movie, an underground movie etc, it would be analyzed five ways to sunday. By saying that Beverley Hills Ninja is his favorite, it can be seen as something amusing and everyone can move on. He surmised that it's the same reason that Terrance Malick said that one of his favorite movies is Zoolander.

Terrence Malick also said one of his favorite films was Smokin' Aces. Picturing this arty, recluse guy watching a Tarantino knock off film and then finding it's one of his favorite films is extremely funny.

Even Kubrick love Chaplin (specifically City Light). I think its possibly because they are somewhat childhood favorites for them or that even with all the stylings they have is not relatively representative of their taste in their film. In fact, (according to a letterboxd list) he seems to have a record of saying appreciating For Your Eyes Only' (1981) too.

I also think that Chaplin has been the relatively popular film favorite for a lot of high-brow filmmakers during the early parts of the 20th century. He is always highly respected since he is probably one of the earliest and most famous examples of film auteurs too. Thematically, his films are timely and never went for easy jabs.

So first of all, every single auteur of his generation loved Chaplin. And I'm not exaggerating at all, look at the top favorites of any filmmaker born in the early 1900s, they have at least one Chaplin, be it Dreyer, de Sica, Wyler, Powell, Lean, Renoir, whoever.

He was most likely a big part of their childhood as cinephiles, the first director whose name they knew. So there is a nostalgia factor.

Some words from Tarkovsky, who felt even more strongly about this than Bresson:

"And is Chaplin—comedy? No: he is Chaplin, pure and simple; a unique phenomenon, never to be repeated. He is unadulterated hyperbole; but above all he stuns us at every moment of his screen existence with the truth of his hero’s behavior. In the most absurd situation Chaplin is completely natural; and that is why he is funny."

If you watch Bresson’s movies, he really likes to play the physical realities of his stories out to the fullest. Like at the beginning of Pickpocket, he shows Michel taking his time getting close to the woman, waiting for the right moment to unbuckle the purse, pausing as the latch comes undone, trying not to be noticed, slowly grabbing the money, then quickly blending into the crowd. There’s a logical chain of action that he’s created there.

Chaplin basically does the same thing. He doesn’t rush through scenes or the story. Everything that happens is fully played out before he moves onto the next thing. Again, there is a logic to the physical reality that Chaplin creates.
I believe Jim Jarmusch recently said Atomic Blonde was one of his favorites. Just goes to show you

Chaplin style of performance may have derived from Vaudeville. But his craft was completely cinematic. Think of the greatest moments in his ouvre such as the ending of City Lights. These are uniquely cinematic moments. Chaplin was received in his time by great modernist artists as one of their peers, a practically unequaled modern artist working in this emerging art form. It’s not hard to see why Bresson, a filmaker who prioritised preformance and mise-en-scene found a great deal of influence in Chaplin, who pushed the art form forward with naturalist performances in films like A Woman in New York.

It's the economy of means IMO. 1 actor + 1 camera = magic. Bresson understood better than anyone that Chaplin's is a cinema of patience and endless retakes until you reach a few feet of filmed sublimity. On stage in the theater you don't get retakes! I believe it's as simple as that. Since with film you have the option of doing retakes until you achieve goodness, you kind of have an obligation to do so! And Chaplin is surely the greatest example of this — dude owned his own physical studio with a year-round full time employed staff for 20+ years solely so he could have total control how his performances got recorded! 

For me, it's kind of easy to imagine a person who lived through Chaplin as essentially equating everything that is good and desirable in cinema with Chaplin. 

I sometimes myself put The Cure at the #1 spot solely for the revolving door gag. I mean, the shit is NUTS.

It was Kubrick who also said that Chaplin is all content and no style.

Chaplin typically films himself as film makers filmed Astaire: at an appropriate distance to see his full body (after all, many of his moves are dance-like)--few closeups; and even in frenetic scenes the pace is leisurely so the audience can absorb all of it and knows where everything is in relation to everything else.
and Zoolander

I'm a bit late to the party. I don't know if anyone will read this...

Many people made some very good points about the technical similarities in style, but I think the decisive factor is that the true masters of cinema such as Bresson, Tarkovsky, etc. recognize how difficult it is to reach that highest level of purity (of emotional expression), such as you can find in City Lights (in other Chaplins films too, but specifically in City Lights).

Another movie that is often seen in the top 10 lists of great directors is Ozu's "Tokyo Story," probably for the same reasons, even though it's very different in style. 

For example, we can find the same kind of thing in jazz music, too. Some of the most progressive and experimental artists (such as Gil Evans) have named Louis Armstrong to be their greatest influence.

For a long time after the advent of sound in film, silent films were considered to be more artistic because of how much more creativity had to go into creating a narrative. 

Also, Bresson was a master of sound and careful use of it himself. I remember watching A Man Escaped in our sound week in my film class and analyzing how the use of sound (and sometimes lack of it) played a key role in moving the narrative forward.

> Chaplin style of performance may have derived from Vaudeville. But his craft was completely cinematic. 

This is a really good insight, because if you compare him to someone like Groucho Marx and his brothers you see they just adapted Vaudeville for film, they didn't really transcend the medium. I love the Marx brothers, I think Harpo's physical comedy is one of the best, but they relied heavily on the theatrical style they had their start in. Marx's famous greasepaint mustache and eyebrows are a perfect example, something that started so the theater cheapseats could recognize him became his persona even into the film era because that was how he operated.
I almost spit out my popcorn at this one! Imagine Malick watching Zoolander in his trailer waiting to shoot scenes in Tree of Life or something.
To clarify on this one, Malick just mentioned Smoking Aces as something he had seen recently that he really enjoyed, not that it was one of his favourite films of all time.

With Bresson, it's hard to say.

Being a perpetual adolescent - like Chaplin - he might have felt a deep connection that he played off as a film vs. theater thing, when really it was more basic/visceral.

His form as noted above is classic BBB - Bad Boy Bresson - and shows all the trademarks of the rebellious teenager he always was.

To be a little more charitable, both were bare bones filmmakers, though CC gave in to his sentimentalism while RB fought it by papering over his Chaplinesque setups with teenage cynicism.

Who knew I'd find a Bresson thread the minute I signed up!

Fascinating/brilliant/awful guy.

What is square punching

Instead of framing a person on 1/3 or 2/3 line of a rectangular frame (like 1.85:1 or 1.37:1) so there’s a nice orientation when cutting back and forth during coverage, you centre the subject dead centre in the middle of the frame. It’s really unusual to see and since widescreen became the normal is basically never done anymore, so it massively sticks out whenever you see it.
